conditionality: A single source carries the whole row, so there is no cross-source check on it. effect_mechanism: What an establishment bill buys depends on the wetland type and on how much hydrological work it needs. In a large tropical peat rewetting trial, where dams are built in large volumes the construction cost per compacted-peat canal dam is estimated at about 300 US$, which the authors call very economical compared with rewetting methods using wood and other materials brought in from elsewhere [ev_project_cost_hooi24_4]. A global meta-analysis of restoration costs gives median total project costs per hectare per year of the restoration event, in 2010 US$: US$89 660 for saltmarsh [ev_project_cost_tail20w1_6], US$71 221 for freshwater marsh [ev_project_cost_tail20w1_9], US$20 948 for floodplains [ev_project_cost_tail20w1_7] and US$1229 for peatlands [ev_project_cost_tail20w1_8]. Read ordinally, marsh restoration, which may need more hydrological manipulation such as weirs, is the expensive end and peatland rewetting the cheap end.

justification.mechanism: What an establishment bill buys depends on the wetland type and on how much hydrological work it needs. In a large tropical peat rewetting trial, where dams are built in large volumes the construction cost per compacted-peat canal dam is estimated at about 300 US$, which the authors call very economical compared with rewetting methods using wood and other materials brought in from elsewhere [ev_project_cost_hooi24_4]. A global meta-analysis of restoration costs gives median total project costs per hectare per year of the restoration event, in 2010 US$: US$89 660 for saltmarsh [ev_project_cost_tail20w1_6], US$71 221 for freshwater marsh [ev_project_cost_tail20w1_9], US$20 948 for floodplains [ev_project_cost_tail20w1_7] and US$1229 for peatlands [ev_project_cost_tail20w1_8]. effect_mechanism: Two kinds of recurring cost sit in this pool. The first is a land payment in a US national model: where wetlands are restored on farmland, land rental costs cover the opportunity cost of land removed from agricultural production, and for cropland they are, in the mean, more than five times greater than those for pastureland, at US$274 ± 156 per hectare [ev_project_cost_cheng20_6]. Design, construction and maintenance enter the same framework as area-dependent costs annualised over a 50-year management horizon at a real discount rate of 4%, with the rental rates taken from state-level agricultural statistics across the 48 contiguous states. The second is upkeep: evidence compiled in the cost-effectiveness review suggests that annual monitoring costs are typically around 20% of the initial restoration investment for floodplain restoration in the USA, and mangrove restoration in the Philippines and Vietnam [ev_project_cost_tail20w1_11].
conditionality: This is a modelled national cost framework for constructed nutrient-retention wetlands, and the recurring item prices forgone agriculture on US cropland, a high-income economy; it cannot be read across to a low- or lower-middle-income landscape, where the opportunity cost of farmland is set by quite different land and tenure arrangements. No currency year is stated in the quoted passage. The monitoring share is a cited summary, not a measurement from these projects, and it is expressed relative to the initial investment, so it scales with however large that establishment cost was. The useful point is structural: where wetlands are restored on farmland, the standing cost is the production forgone, not the upkeep of the works. The Taillardat per-hectare-per-year medians formerly pooled here are total project capital annualised over the restoration event and now sit in establishment cost (the cost-routing rule) [ev_project_cost_cheng20_6].
